Issues.Title: Migrate FabricBot Tasks to Config-as-Code
Issues.Body:
**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/coreclr) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/coreclr) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

[*Pull Request Create*](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/prcreate), a [MerlinBot](https://https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot) Extension, was used to automatically create this pull request. If you have any questions or concerns with this pull request, please contact [MerlinBot Expert DRI](mailto:merlinbotdri@microsoft.com).

Issues.Title: Migrate FabricBot Tasks to Config-as-Code
Issues.Body:
**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/cli) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/cli) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

[*Pull Request Create*](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/prcreate), a [MerlinBot](https://https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot) Extension, was used to automatically create this pull request. If you have any questions or concerns with this pull request, please contact [MerlinBot Expert DRI](mailto:merlinbotdri@microsoft.com).

Issues.Title: Confusing behavior when using AssemblyInfo.cs
Issues.Body:
I'm completely perplexed.

I created a .Net Standard 2.0 library project.

I explicity added an AssemblyInfo.cs file, we need this because we use this utility to "stamp" our assemblies when we build them:

https://github.com/ygoe/NetRevisionTool

That utility is run as a pre/post build event and temporarily replaces placeholders in the AssemblyInformationalVersion attribute with runtime values (like repo folder name, commit ID, branch etc etc).

The completed assembly then has this info "burned" into it as we go forward.

.Net Standard is not working with this.

1. It seems to populatethe Package Version (in the project's Package section) with whatever we put into AssemblyInfo.cs for AssemblyInformationalVersion.
2. The version of the generated nuget package is always set as 1.0.0.

This is just mind blowing, is there no way we can do this seemingly simple operation any more if adopt .Net Standard?

Issues.Title: Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions
Issues.Body:
I was looking through this repository to determine if .NET Standard 2.1 libraries support default interface methods - it looks like they do, given the presence of `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.RuntimeFeature.DefaultImplementationsOfInterfaces`, as well as my own experimenting in VS 2019. It seems I was mistaken when thinking that this was not the case, so I'm glad this repository is easily accessible to determine this.

But while doing this, I found it difficult to determine what commits were included in this particular .NET Standard version. I see that there's a tag `v2.1.0-prerelease.19126.1`, as well as branches `release/2.0.0`, `release/3.0`, and `release/3.0-preview9`. One of the machines I tested VS 2019 on had a `netstandard.dll` assembly, itself targeting .NETStandard v2.1.0, with AssemblyInformationalVersion `1.1.0+a5b5f2e1e369972c8ff1e2183979fab6099f52ef`; this commit is part of the `release/3.0` branch. However, another machine had a same-named assembly, targeting .NETCoreApp v3.0 and AssemblyInformationalVersion `3.0.0+4ac4c0367003fe3973a3648eb0715ddb0e3bbcea`, and I don't see that commit hash in this repository.

Additionally, [this blog post](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/the-future-of-net-standard/) states that 2.1 will be the last version, but there is another prerelease tag `v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1` and [on GitHub](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/releases/tag/v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1) it's labelled .NET 5.0 Preview 2.

So I have a few questions for understanding this repository:

1. Since .NET Standard 2.1 is released, are there plans to continue development in this repository for e.g. the shared BCL going forward with .NET 5+?
2. Are there multiple kinds of `netstandard.dll` for a single .NET Standard version? E.g. are there separate versions for .NET Framework to reference and for .NET Core / .NET 5+ to reference?
3. Do the tags / branch names in this repository correspond to a .NET Standard version or something else?
4. It looks like there are patch releases; are there patch versions of a single .NET Standard version?
5. Are there other repositories which are being used to create `netstandard.dll`?
6. Is there a way to determine, from the repository, which commit is the one used for a given release?

Thank you for your consideration.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions" (#1777)

Issues.Title: Issue with resolving between .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1
Issues.Body:
# Summary

.NET Standard version is not resolved correctly when a transitive dependency targets multiple .NET Standard versions.

# Environment

- Windows 10 (19042.746)
- .NET 5 SDK 5.0.201

# Minimal reproducible example
[bug.zip](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/files/6209239/bug.zip)

This is a three-project solution:
- `TestProject1` targeting `netcoreapp3.1`
- `ClassProject1` targeting `netstandard2.0`
- `ClassProject2` targeting *both* `netstandard2.0` and `netstandard2.1`

The project dependency chain is: `TestProject1 -> ClassProject1 -> ClassProject2`

A method (`ClassProject2Test1`) on `ClassProject2` is hidden behind a `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.

# The issue

The unit test failed with a `MissingMethodException`

```
[xUnit.net 00:00:00.38]     TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [FAIL]
  Failed TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [2 ms]
  Error Message:
   System.MissingMethodException : Method not found: 'Void ClassLibrary2.Class2.Class2Test1()'.
  Stack Trace:
     at ClassLibrary1.Class1.Class1Test1()
   at TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1() in C:\Users\rex\source\netstandard-bug-repro\TestProject1\UnitTest1.cs:line 12
```

# Expected result

The compiler should have resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.0)*` 

# Actual result

The compiler resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.1)*` 

Which causes the exception because the offending method, `ClassProject2Test1`, was hidden by the `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Issue with resolving between .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1" (#1787)

Issues.Title: Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions
Issues.Body:
### Problem
There is a security vulnerability with the version of System.Text.RegularExpressions that is used by dotnet standard. The vulnerable version of System.Text.RegularExpressions is 4.3.0. Please see links below for the vulnerability documentation or discussion:

https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/en-US/vulnerability/CVE-2019-0820
https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/111
https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2019-0820
https://snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-DOTNET-SYSTEMTEXTREGULAREXPRESSIONS-174708
https://www.whitesourcesoftware.com/vulnerability-database/CVE-2019-0820

The dotnet commit that fixed the vulnerability is https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/commit/19d4b1163d8a03dd90ff5fd1785eea6305112545

### Issue:
We use whitesource and it has caught this issue with high severity. We don't consume System.Text.RegularExpressions directly but packages that use this. Therefore as a transitive dependency due to NetStandard library, which is being used by several other dotnet packages like Castle Windsor, MassTransit etc., Once an update is available the others could followup and update.

### Code:

[The latest version 2.0.3 of Net standard ](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) still seem to be using System.Text.RegularExpressions version 4.3.0 as per https://github.com/dotnet/standard/blob/master/src/apicompat/netstandard/netstandard.depproj

### Fix
Please update[ library](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) targeting .netStandard 1.6 to update System.Text.RegularExpression package to latest secured version 4.3.1 to fix the security issue or kindly suggest alternatives.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions" (#1786)

Issues.Title: linq using GetValueOrDefault  in Where clause problem
Issues.Body:
Hello,

I am currently using .NET core 2.2.x and EF Core. 2.2.6. I have a function that returns a List<Animal> from the database with no issue. It returns 11 results. However, when I try to use `.Where(p => p.DeletedAt.GetValueOrDefault(DateTime.Now) => DateTime.Now).ToList()`, it still should return 11 results, however it returns 0. I also eliminated the possibility that there is something wrong with my where clause (logic) because it works perfectly on 4.6.1 EF Core 2.2.6. Furthermore, I confirmed that it is only where I am comparing a nullable type using that function and I am guessing that I missed a thread someone opened on this issue. I am aware .NET core 2.2 is not LTS. I also thought this goes here because it's not AFAIK, an EF core issue but rather an Ienumerable/Linq issue.

Update: As it turns out your notion of `DateTime.Now` getting evaluated twice is true. To rectify that, I will now be using `DateTime.Now.Date`. This is odd because this exact code works on 4.6.1. You're probably right. SMH. Thank you @GrabYourPitchforks! You may now close.

Issues.Title: System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings slow
Issues.Body:
_This issue has been moved from [a ticket on Developer Community](https://developercommunity2.visualstudio.com/t/SystemDrawingPrintingPrinterSettings-/890524)._ --- Hello I'm debugging a problem with the printer settings. Some calls are significant slower if the default printer is a network printer, even if I explicit set a local printer name. After studying referencesource I think I found the culprit. I call: var printerSettings = new System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings(); printerSettings.PrinterName = "LOCALPRINTER"; // the next call is slow if the OS default printer is a network printer var res = printerSettings.DefaultPageSettings.PrinterResolution Internally FastDeviceCapabilities is called. FastDeviceCapabilities calls GetOutputPort. But GetOutput port return the port of the default printer and not the port of the given printer! In addition, DeviceCapabilities is then called with a wrong combination of printer name and port, don't know if this could lead to additional problems. Resolution: GetOutputPort should return the port of the given printer and not accessing the default printer at all. Issues.Title: Build issues when referencing project that targets multiple frameworks C# WPF
Issues.Body:
I'm working on converting a large WPF solution's projects to SDK style and ran into some issues.

The solution is large with multiple projects(old style) all targeting .net452 and some nugets(some made by me) installed, targeting both .net452 and .netstandard2.1 This all seems to work fine, somehow the nuget manages to install the correct version targeting .net452.

I have decided to slowly convert the projects inside the solution to SDK style targeting .net452 and .netstandard2.1 just like the nugets.

This is where the problem starts, one project was converted so far that is referenced by multiple other projects. Localy everything seems to build and run fine, however when Azure DevOps(VS version 2019) is used to build the solution there are 2 scenarios:

1. The famous error message is shown:

                "Error CS0012: The type 'Object' is defined in an assembly that is not referenced. You must add a reference to assembly 
                 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0"

2. It builds fine but on app launch it crashes with:

                 "Could not load file or assembly 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=cc7b13ffcd2ddd51' 
                 or one of its dependencies. The system cannot find the file specified."

I'm suspecting that the problem is related to referencing the SDK project, it looks like that somehow it references the .netstandard2.1 instead of the .net452.

The reason this is my suspicion is that if targetframework is set to only .net452 on the referenced project everything works fine. Google has led me to two possible solutions to tell the project what framework to use from the reference:

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj"
                  AdditionalProperties="TargetFramework=net452">
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
and

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj">
      <SetTargetFramework>TargetFramework=net452</SetTargetFramework>
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <<Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
This doesn't look like it's doing anything and the problem still persists. At the moment I ran out of ideas and I'm here asking for help. Please let me know what I'm doing wrong or what else I can try.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Build issues when referencing project that targets multiple frameworks C# WPF" (#1776)

As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

Issues.Title: Fix RSA OAEP decryption in OpenSSL with non-power-of-two keys lengths
Issues.Body:
## Customer Impact

A customer reported in dotnet/runtime#71607 that decrypting RSA OAEP with SHA2 and a 3072-bit key on Linux resulted in a OAEP de-padding error, while other platforms were able to perform these operations successfully.

Investigation in to the issue led to uncover that RSA OAEP decryption that uses the managed implementation does not work with non-power-of-two keys because we do not slice a rented buffer accordingly. The current implementation only works because `CryptoPool.Rent` happens to give back power-of-two arrays which are exactly the same size as the key.

The fix is to slice the data to the correct size.

This does not affect dotnet/runtime because the managed implementation of RSA OAEP is no longer used for OpenSSL RSA decryption. This change was introduced in dotnet/runtime#50063.

## Testing

Unit tests were introduced to test RSA OAEP encryption with a 3072-bit RSA key. These tests will be forward-ported to dotnet/runtime.

## Risk

Minimal. The change is localized and understood that a `Slice` was missing.

Issues.Title: Introduce a new pool for large Razor tag helper collection lists
Issues.Body:
Tag helper collection builders are already pooled, but the dumps in https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Significant-intellisense-lag-when-adding/11169845 showed that there are some downsides to this, in the real world. Instead of repeatedly trimming large descriptor lists and growing them again for the next document, or missing the pool entirely due to large descriptor counts, this PR introduces a separate pool of 8 slows for large tag helper lists.

The results look good in isolation, with a downside of 2mb of additional list storage and extra growth allocations for larger cold namespace lists. Will see what DDRITs have to say too.

Scenario | Allocated before | Allocated after
-- | -- | --
Reuse a builder with 4,096 descriptors | 49,232 B | 32 B
Reuse a builder with 8,192 descriptors | 114,792 B | 32 B
Reuse 16 pooled lists with 8,192 descriptors each | 1,836,160 B | 918,080 B
Create a namespace list with 4 descriptors | 1,080 B | 88 B
Create a namespace list with 128 descriptors | 1,080 B | 2,192 B

 ###### Microsoft Reviewers: [Open in CodeFlow](https://microsoft.github.io/open-pr/?codeflow=https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/pull/86217)

Issues.Title: Avoid intermediate strings in Razor component code generation
Issues.Body:
Sadly there were no improvements possible to the major string allocations in the dumps in https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Significant-intellisense-lag-when-adding/11169845 but I found these little ones while looking anyway.

Scenario | Before | After | Saved
-- | -- | -- | --
Single 512-character HTML content token | 1,048 B | 0 B | 1,048 B (100%)
Single 512-character HTML attribute value | 1,496 B | 448 B | 1,048 B (70%)
Generic method emission with three cascading type parameters | 1,200 B | 992 B | 208 B (17%)
Generic method emission with one cascading type parameter | 1,104 B | 992 B | 112 B (10%)

Existing test coverage includes all of the scenarios being modified here.
 ###### Microsoft Reviewers: [Open in CodeFlow](https://microsoft.github.io/open-pr/?codeflow=https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/pull/86203)
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed or merged PR "Avoid intermediate strings in Razor component code generation" (#86203)

Issues.Title: Reduce allocations from Razor type inference
Issues.Body:
In the dumps in https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Significant-intellisense-lag-when-adding/11169845 there were allocations showing up in handling generic components to do with `.ToList()` and `.OfType()` usage. This replaces those with pooled lists, and a custom struct enumerator. I also rolled the changes out to other places with the same pattern, that didn't strictly show up in the dumps.

Reductions are up to about 55% depending on the complexity of the Razor code being compiled, though to be fair some of the improvements are only around 5%.

Issues.Title: Keep the margin menu open when toggling inheritance
Issues.Body: The editor margin context menu closes after toggling Show Inheritance, forcing users to reopen it to adjust other margin options. This unlike the other menu items in the menu, which do keep the menu open. This PR does two things: - Marks this command with `KeepMenuOpen`, a new feature in VSCT, that leaves the parent menu open after executing. - Also marked it `TogglePatternAvailable` so that its exposed as a toggle to UI Automation and ensures that the command-system refreshes its check state after each click while the menu remains open. The command requires a newer VSCT compiler, so this also pins a compatible VSSDK build toolset. The newer build tools introduced a bug [VSIX builds fail with project-reference aliases after upgrading to VSSDK 18.9](https://devdiv.visualstudio.com/DevDiv/_workitems/edit/3085133) so I needed to move VSIX manifest tokens over to project file names to workaround it. ###### Microsoft Reviewers: [Open in CodeFlow](https://microsoft.github.io/open-pr/?codeflow=https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/pull/86201)

Issues.Title: Compiler output cache drops warnings and changes MSBuild -warnaserror results
Issues.Body:
The experimental compiler output cache drops warnings on cache hits. With MSBuild's engine-level `-warnaserror`, the compiler can succeed while the build fails. The server caches that result, so the next identical rebuild incorrectly succeeds.

**Version Used**: .NET SDK `11.0.100-rc.1.26420.103`, C# compiler `5.11.0-1.26420.103`, Linux x64.

**Steps to Reproduce**:

In a fresh directory, create `CacheWarningRepro.csproj`:

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net11.0</TargetFramework>
    <UseSharedCompilation>true</UseSharedCompilation>
    <Features>use-global-cache=$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory)compiler-cache</Features>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

And `C.cs`:

```csharp
public class C
{
    [System.Obsolete("Example warning")]
    public static void Old() { }

    public static void M() => Old();
}
```

Run the same command twice:

```sh
dotnet build -t:Rebuild -warnaserror
dotnet build -t:Rebuild -warnaserror
```

**Diagnostic Id**: `CS0618`.

**Expected Behavior**: Both rebuilds fail with `CS0618` promoted to an error.

**Actual Behavior**: The first rebuild fails with exit code 1. The second restores the compiler outputs from cache, reports no warnings or errors, and succeeds with exit code 0. Both invocations reach the compiler server; this is not MSBuild's incremental target skipping.

This is distinct from compiler-owned `TreatWarningsAsErrors`: MSBuild applies its policy after receiving the compiler result. Replaying the original compiler warnings on cache hits would preserve that downstream decision without including MSBuild warning policy in the compiler cache key.

> *This content was created with assistance from AI.*

Issues.Title: Investigate eliminating unused synthesized struct `this` loads in async methods
Issues.Body:
Follow-up to the extra-load discussion on dotnet/roslyn#86134.

An async struct method can emit a load of `this` even when its source body never references the receiver:

```csharp
struct S
{
    public async Task<int> M(int value)
    {
        await Task.Delay(1);
        return value;
    }
}
```

With runtime-async lowering, the method starts with:

```il
ldarg.0
ldobj S
pop
```

`RuntimeAsyncRewriter.hoistThisIfNeeded` synthesizes a copy of the struct receiver. With the changes in dotnet/roslyn#86134, removing the unused local preserves the dereference, leaving this load behind. The PR discussion also identifies analogous receiver copying in traditional async lowering.

We should investigate whether compiler-generated receiver reads can be distinguished from reads required by user code, allowing unnecessary loads to be optimized away.

The investigation should:
- Cover runtime-async and traditional state-machine lowering.
- Preserve dereferences corresponding to source-level reads, including an explicit `_ = this;`.
- Add focused IL and execution coverage for whichever optimizations are safe.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "Investigate eliminating unused synthesized struct `this` loads in async methods" (#86195)

Issues.Title: CS8629 and CS8604 are reported despite null checks after three left joins in query syntax
Issues.Body:
**Version Used**: 
.NET SDK 10.0.401  
C# compiler/MSBuild 18.9.11+e34a38d2ae  

**Description**:
Nullable flow analysis reports `CS8629: Nullable value type may be null` and `CS8604: Possible null reference argument for parameter` for nullable property accesses guarded by not-null checks in a LINQ query expression after three chained left joins.

The same query expressed with the corresponding LINQ method calls produces neither of the two warnings.

When the query is reduced to one or two chained left joins, the warnings are not produced.

**Steps to Reproduce**:
```csharp

#nullable enable

using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;

public sealed class Item
{
	public int Id { get; init; }
	public int? A { get; init; }
	public string? B { get; init; }
}

public sealed record Pair(int A, string B);

public static class Repro
{
	public static IEnumerable<Pair?> QuerySyntax(
		IEnumerable<int> ids,
		IEnumerable<Item> items,
		IEnumerable<int> first,
		IEnumerable<int> second) =>
		from id in ids
		join item in items on id equals item.Id into itemGroup
		from item in itemGroup.DefaultIfEmpty()
		join a in first on item.Id equals a into firstGroup
		from a in firstGroup.DefaultIfEmpty()
		join b in second on a equals b into secondGroup
		from b in secondGroup.DefaultIfEmpty()
		select item.A != null && item.B != null
			? new Pair(item.A.Value, item.B) // CS8629 and CS8604
			: null;

	public static IEnumerable<Pair?> MethodSyntax(
		IEnumerable<int> ids,
		IEnumerable<Item> items,
		IEnumerable<int> first,
		IEnumerable<int> second) =>
		ids
			.GroupJoin(
				items,
				id => id,
				item => item.Id,
				(id, itemGroup) => new { id, itemGroup })
			.SelectMany(
				x => x.itemGroup.DefaultIfEmpty(),
				(x, item) => new { item })
			.GroupJoin(
				first,
				x => x.item!.Id,
				a => a,
				(x, firstGroup) => new { x.item, firstGroup })
			.SelectMany(
				x => x.firstGroup.DefaultIfEmpty(),
				(x, a) => new { x.item, a })
			.GroupJoin(
				second,
				x => x.a,
				b => b,
				(x, secondGroup) => new { x.item, secondGroup })
			.SelectMany(
				x => x.secondGroup.DefaultIfEmpty(),
				(x, _) => x.item)
			.Select(item => item!.A != null && item.B != null
				? new Pair(item.A.Value, item.B) // no diagnostics
				: null);
}
```

**Diagnostic Id**:
CS8629: Nullable value type may be null.
CS8604: Possible null reference argument for parameter

**Expected Behavior**:
Compiling should not produce a warning because the properties are checked for null.

**Actual Behavior**:
Compiling produces two warnings:
> warning CS8629: Nullable value type may be null.
> warning CS8604: Possible null reference argument for parameter
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "CS8629 and CS8604 are reported despite null checks after three left joins in query syntax" (#86188)

Issues.Title: Fix TemplateVerifier CLI outside test runners
Issues.Body:
🤖 This PR is part of the weekly test issue cleanup effort.

Fixes the TemplateVerifier CLI failure caused by routing directory verification through `Verify.XunitV3` when no xUnit test context exists. The TemplateVerifier now supplies a runner-independent Verify core adapter, while preserving the existing `DirectoryVerifier` override seam for framework-specific test integrations.

The authoring CLI no longer depends on `Verify.XunitV3`, and the two integration tests tracked by #53889 are re-enabled. The test also covers target-framework uniqueness so the standalone adapter preserves all supported `--unique-for` modes.

Closes #53889

- `Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Authoring.TemplateVerifier.UnitTests` (full project)

```

```

### Steps to reproduce

Issues.Title: [.NET 11 breaking] `dotnet test path\toprojectdir` fails
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

`dotnet test .\test\ProjectDir\` works on .NET 10 SDK but fails on the .NET 11 SDK.

### Steps to reproduce

```
git clone git@github.com:AArnott/Nerdbank.MessagePack.git
cd Nerdbank.MessagePack

# Test .NET 10 SDK
git checkout b13b65ef640a83f166ddf16eb5bffbb74159bd77
dotnet test .\test\Nerdbank.MessagePack.Godot.Tests\

# Test .NET 11 SDK
git checkout 009fc86ccc9208e90f9f9e35e68eaa13caedfa38
dotnet test .\test\Nerdbank.MessagePack.Godot.Tests\
```

### Expected behavior

`dotnet test` runs on both SDK versions.

### Actual behavior

.NET 10 succeeds.
.NET 11 fails:

> Unhandled exception: The project file could not be loaded. Could not find a part of the path 'G:\src\Nerdbank.MessagePack\test\Nerdbank.MessagePack.Godot.Tests\test\Nerdbank.MessagePack.Godot.Tests\Nerdbank.MessagePack.Godot.Tests.csproj'.  G:\src\Nerdbank.MessagePack\test\Nerdbank.MessagePack.Godot.Tests\test\Nerdbank.MessagePack.Godot.Tests\Nerdbank.MessagePack.Godot.Tests.csproj

Note the path doubling. Although the current directory is `G:\src\Nerdbank.MessagePack` and I specified `test\Nerdbank.MessagePack.Godot.Tests` as the relative path to the project directory, the path it expects the project at has the relative path _twice_ is the absolute path.

### Is this a regression?

Yes. .NET 11 regression relative to .NET 10.

### Are there any workarounds?

Yes: switch to the test project directory and run `dotnet test` without a path argument.

Issues.Title: Fix CA2264/CA1871 code fixes for expression-bodied members
Issues.Body:
Fixes #56775

The `ThrowIfNull` fixer assumed the call's parent is a statement. When the call is the whole expression body of a member or local function, the parent is an `ArrowExpressionClauseSyntax`:

| Shape | CA2264 before | CA1871 before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| `void M(int x) => ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(x);` (and ctor, finalizer, `set`/`init` accessor, indexer `set`, local function) | `void M(int x) ;` (CS0501) | fixer throws `InvalidCastException` | block body: empty for CA2264, the `HasValue` check for CA1871 |
| C# lambda `y => ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(y)` | fixer throws `ArgumentNullException` | same path | no fix offered (the diagnostic is still reported) |
| VB `Sub(y) ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(y)` | fixer throws `NullReferenceException` | same path | no fix offered (the diagnostic is still reported) |

The issue says local functions were left unchanged. The tests show they hit the same `;` defect as members, so this PR fixes them too.

### Change

- `DoNotPassNonNullableValueToArgumentNullExceptionThrowIfNull.Fixer.cs` (shared): adds an abstract `CanRewrite(statement)` check. Both `RegisterCodeFixesAsync` and the fix-all `ApplyFix` call it, so a fix-all pass, such as `dotnet format`, also skips the shapes it cannot rewrite. Statement removal moves into a virtual `RemoveStatement` that keeps the current behaviour.
- `CSharpDoNotPassNonNullableValueToArgumentNullExceptionThrowIfNullFixer.cs`: the C# fix can rewrite an `ExpressionStatementSyntax` or an `ArrowExpressionClauseSyntax`. For an arrow clause, it replaces the declaration through `SyntaxGenerator.WithStatements`, which gives an empty block (CA2264) or a block that holds the `if` check (CA1871).
- `BasicDoNotPassNonNullableValueToArgumentNullExceptionThrowIfNullFixer.vb`: the VB fix is not offered when the statement is the body of a `SingleLineLambdaExpressionSyntax`.

Operators, conversion operators, and property or indexer getters are not covered. `ThrowIfNull` returns `void`, so it cannot be the expression body of a member that returns a value.

### Side effect

In C#, the fix is no longer offered when the call is inside a `for` statement's initializer or incrementor list. There, the call's parent is the `ForStatementSyntax`, and the old fix removed the entire loop.

### Tests

All tests are in `DoNotPassStructToArgumentNullExceptionThrowIfNullTests.cs`. Each one is a code-fix test, and each one failed before the fix:

- `NotNullable_ExpressionBodiedMethod_Diagnostic`: the repro from the issue. The method becomes an empty block.
- `NotNullable_ExpressionBodiedConstructor_Diagnostic`
- `NotNullable_ExpressionBodiedDestructor_Diagnostic`
- `NotNullable_ExpressionBodiedAccessor_Diagnostic` (`set`, `init`; C# 9)
- `NotNullable_ExpressionBodiedIndexerAccessor_Diagnostic`
- `NotNullable_ExpressionBodiedLocalFunction_Diagnostic`
- `NotNullable_ExpressionBodiedMethod_TriviaIsPreserved_Diagnostic`: the leading comment and the blank line before the next member are kept. The comment after the removed call is dropped, the same as `TriviaIsNotPreserved_Diagnostic`.
- `Nullable_ExpressionBodiedMethod_Diagnostic`: CA1871 produces a block that holds the `HasValue` check.
- `NotNullable_ExpressionBodiedLambda_Diagnostic`: the diagnostic is reported and no fix is offered.
- `NotNullable_FixAllSkipsExpressionBodiedLambda_Diagnostic`: fix-all fixes the expression-bodied method, leaves the lambda alone, and its diagnostic remains.
- `Vb_NotNullable_SingleLineLambda_Diagnostic`: the diagnostic is reported and no fix is offered.

`Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.NetAnalyzers.UnitTests`: 18,006 passed, 25 skipped, 0 failed. The filtered class has 138 tests, all passing. The analyzer solution builds with 0 warnings. The generated `.md` and `.sarif.template` files are unchanged.

### Not in scope (same fixer, found while probing)

- C# embedded statement: with `if (c) ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(x);`, the fixer throws `ArgumentNullException` (parameter `statement`).
- VB single-line `If`: with `If c Then ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(x)`, the fix produces `If c Then     End Sub`.

I can follow up on these separately if that would help.

Issues.Title: CA2264 code fix produces uncompilable code for an expression-bodied member
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

The CA2264 code fix ("Calling 'ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull' and passing a non-nullable value is a no-op") removes the
call. When the call is the whole body of an expression-bodied member, the fix removes the body as well and leaves a
member declaration with no body, which does not compile (CS0501).

### To Reproduce

SDK 10.0.402, a new class library targeting net10.0:

```csharp
namespace Repro;

public sealed class Sample
{
    public void M(int value) => ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(value);
}
```

`.editorconfig`:

```ini
root = true
[*.cs]
dotnet_diagnostic.CA2264.severity = warning
```

Run:

```
dotnet format analyzers --diagnostics CA2264 --severity warn
dotnet build
```

### Expected behavior

The member still compiles after the fix, for example:

```csharp
public void M(int value) { }
```

### Actual behavior

```csharp
public void M(int value) ;
```

```
error CS0501: 'Sample.M(int)' must declare a body because it is not marked abstract, extern, or partial
```

### Additional context

- The same call in an expression-bodied lambda (`value => ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(value)`) or local function
  is reported but left unchanged by the fix, so only expression-bodied members are affected.
- The fix lives in [`DoNotPassNonNullableValueToArgumentNullExceptionThrowIfNull.Fixer.cs`](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/main/src/Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.NetAnalyzers/src/Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.NetAnalyzers/Microsoft.NetCore.Analyzers/Usage/DoNotPassNonNullableValueToArgumentNullExceptionThrowIfNull.Fixer.cs).
  Removing the invocation statement is right in a block body; for an arrow expression clause it needs to become an
  empty block (or the fix should not be offered there, as for lambdas).
- Found while running `dotnet format` across a solution with CA2264 enabled at warning level.

Issues.Title: PackAsTool with RuntimeIdentifiers and CreateRidSpecificToolPackages=false packs a tool without its implementation
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

A `PackAsTool` project that lists `RuntimeIdentifiers` (for example so a packages lock file covers each RID-specific publish) and sets `CreateRidSpecificToolPackages=false` to get a single framework-dependent tool package produces a package without the tool's program: only `DotnetToolSettings.xml`, under `tools/any/any/`.

`Microsoft.NET.PackTool.targets` decides whether the primary package includes the implementation from `_UserSpecifiedToolPackageRids` (taken from `RuntimeIdentifiers`) and `RuntimeIdentifier` alone:

```xml
<_ToolPackageShouldIncludeImplementation Condition=" '$(_ToolPackageShouldIncludeImplementation)' == '' And '$(PackAsTool)' == 'true' And
                                              ('$(_UserSpecifiedToolPackageRids)' == ''
                                                 or '$(RuntimeIdentifier)' != '')">true</_ToolPackageShouldIncludeImplementation>
```

`CreateRidSpecificToolPackages` is not consulted, so with it set to `false` no RID-specific packages are made and the primary package is a pointer to packages that do not exist. #51281 (for #51199) added the opt-out for `RuntimeIdentifier`; this is the `RuntimeIdentifiers` case. The same lines are on `main` and `release/10.0.4xx` (read from source).

### Steps to reproduce

`Tool.csproj`:

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <PackAsTool>true</PackAsTool>
    <ToolCommandName>repro</ToolCommandName>
    <RuntimeIdentifiers>win-x64;linux-x64</RuntimeIdentifiers>
    <CreateRidSpecificToolPackages>false</CreateRidSpecificToolPackages>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

`Program.cs`:

```cs
System.Console.WriteLine("hello");
```

Run `dotnet pack -o out` and list the package's `tools/` entries.

### Expected behavior

A framework-dependent, RID-agnostic tool package as without `RuntimeIdentifiers`: `tools/net10.0/any/Tool.dll`, its dependencies and `DotnetToolSettings.xml` naming `Tool.dll`.

### Actual behavior

`dotnet pack` exits 0 and `Tool.1.0.0.nupkg` contains only `tools/any/any/DotnetToolSettings.xml`. No RID-specific packages are produced, so the tool cannot be installed or run.

### Is this a regression?

Yes, by the .NET 10 tool packaging change: before RID-specific tool packages, `RuntimeIdentifiers` did not change what a tool package contained. Not tested here with a .NET 9 SDK.

### Are there any workarounds?

Leave `RuntimeIdentifiers` out of the pack's build evaluation, for example `Condition="'$(_IsPacking)' != 'true' or '$(MSBuildIsRestoring)' == 'true'"`, which relies on an internal property. Setting `_ToolPackageShouldIncludeImplementation=true` (made settable in #50015) is another, also internal.

### dotnet --info output

```
.NET SDK:
 Version:           10.0.402
 Commit:            a8dd0577c5
 MSBuild version:   18.9.15+a8dd0577c

Runtime Environment:
 OS Name:     Windows
 OS Version:  10.0.26200
 RID:         win-x64

Host:
  Version:      10.0.13
```

### IDE version

None (command line).

Issues.Title: dotnet publish <sln> --no-build -m:1 silently omits ProjectReference assemblies when a referencing project is published first
Issues.Body:
### Issue Description

When a solution is published with `--no-build` on a single MSBuild node, an Exe project that is referenced by another project (for example, a test project) can be published without the assemblies of its own `ProjectReference`s. The publish succeeds with no errors or warnings. `<App>.deps.json` lists the referenced project, but its `.dll` is missing from the publish directory, so the app fails at startup with `FileNotFoundException`.

In our CI (TeamCity, `mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0` container limited to 1 CPU), this produced a broken Docker image after we only added a test project that references a console app.

[msbuild-repro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33901394/msbuild-repro.zip)

### Steps to Reproduce

Minimal repro (3 projects, no packages): 

[msbuild-repro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33901404/msbuild-repro.zip)

- `Lib` — class library
- `App` — `OutputType=Exe`, `ProjectReference` → `Lib`
- `App.Tests` — `ProjectReference` → `App`, listed in the `.sln` **before** `App`

```sh
dotnet build   Repro.sln -c Release -m:1
dotnet publish Repro.sln -c Release --no-build -m:1
ls App/bin/Release/net8.0/publish
```


### Expected Behavior

`App/bin/Release/net8.0/publish` contains `Lib.dll`, the same as when `App` is published alone.


### Actual Behavior

```
App
App.deps.json
App.dll
App.pdb
App.runtimeconfig.json
```

`Lib.dll` is missing. There is no error or warning.


### Analysis

From a diagnostic log (`-v:diag`) of the failing case:

1. The solution publishes `App.Tests` first. Its `_PublishNoBuildAlternative` calls `GetCopyToPublishDirectoryItems` on `App`. Because of `--no-build`, `App` has not been built in this invocation, so this is the first target that runs in the `App` project instance.
2. `GetCopyToPublishDirectoryItems` (Microsoft.NET.Publish.targets) has `DependsOnTargets="AssignTargetPaths; DefaultCopyToPublishDirectoryMetadata; ...; _SplitProjectReferencesByFileExistence; _GetProjectReferenceTargetFrameworkProperties"`. `AssignProjectConfiguration` is not in that list, so `_SplitProjectReferencesByFileExistence` runs while `@(ProjectReferenceWithConfiguration)` is still empty. `@(_MSBuildProjectReferenceExistent)` is computed as empty, and the target is marked as built.
3. The solution then runs `Publish` on the **same** `App` instance (same global properties). `AssignProjectConfiguration` now fills `ProjectReferenceWithConfiguration` with `Lib`, but `_SplitProjectReferencesByFileExistence` is skipped: `Previously built successfully`. `ResolveProjectReferences` therefore sees an empty `_MSBuildProjectReferenceExistent`, and every `MSBuild` task in it is skipped:

   ```
   Task "MSBuild" skipped, due to false condition; ('%(_MSBuildProjectReferenceExistent.BuildReference)' == 'true' and '@(ProjectReferenceWithConfiguration)' != '' ...) was evaluated as ('' == 'true' and '../Lib/Lib.csproj' != '' ...)
   ```

4. `Lib.dll` never gets into `ReferenceCopyLocalPaths` / `ResolvedFileToPublish`, so it is not copied to the publish directory.

Without `--no-build`, or when `App` is published before anyone calls `GetCopyToPublishDirectoryItems` on it, `AssignProjectConfiguration` runs before `_SplitProjectReferencesByFileExistence` and the result is correct.


### Versions & Configurations

- .NET SDK 8.0.426 (`mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0`), 9.0.102, 10.0.402 — Linux x64 containers
- .NET SDK 10.0.302 — Windows 11 x64

Issues.Title: dotnetup init: label the platform-recommended access mode separately from the preselected configured mode
Issues.Body:
## Problem

When dotnetup is already configured, `dotnetup init` preselects the configured access mode and labels it `(default)`. For example, if `dotnetup.config.json` contains `"accessMode": "none"`, the form shows `None  (default)` on Windows, even though the platform default for new setups on Windows is `Everywhere`.

This happens because `InitDefaultsResolver.GetDefaultAccessMode` gives a supported configured mode priority over the platform default. `InitFormModel.BuildAccessModeField` then uses that mode as the field's `DefaultIndex`, which is rendered with the `(default)` suffix. Users who reconfigure can't tell which mode dotnetup recommends for their platform.

## Proposal

Keep preselecting the configured mode, so accepting the form without edits preserves the current setup. Label the two modes separately:

- `(current)` on the configured mode
- `(recommended)` on the platform default (`Everywhere` on Windows; `Shell` elsewhere when a supported shell is detected, otherwise `None`)

When the two are the same, show a single label. "Changed from default" highlighting should compare against the current (preselected) mode.

Issues.Title: Delete stale RID-specific assets file between local tool restores
Issues.Body:
The order in which I declared my tools in the dotnet-tools.json should not matter. But it did. With `aspire.cli` listed before `csharpier` in `dotnet-tools.json`, a fresh restore fails. The error says the `csharpier` package only contains `aspire`.

I tasked Claude to fix this bug, and this is the result.

The bug is in `dotnet tool restore`. Every local tool in one restore shares one asset directory. A RID-specific tool like _aspire.cli_ leaves `project.assets.ridpackage.json` behind. The next tool, _csharpier_, picks it up and fails.

A helper in `ToolPackageDownloaderBase.cs` deletes that stale file before the next tool's assets are written. A manual restore with the patched build succeeded for both tools.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open PR "Delete stale RID-specific assets file between local tool restores" (#56763)

Issues.Title: .NET October 2026 out-of-band security updates
Issues.Body:
On October 25, 2026, we released out-of-band security updates for .NET 8.0.33, .NET 9.0.22, .NET 10.0.14, and .NET 11 Release Candidate 3 (prerelease). We recommend updating affected applications and build environments as soon as possible. .NET Framework is not affected.

## Release Notes

* [Release details and feedback](https://github.com/dotnet/core/issues/10660)
* [.NET 8.0.33 and .NET SDK 8.0.133 / 8.0.427](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/8.0/8.0.33/8.0.33.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/8.0))
* [.NET 9.0.22 and .NET SDK 9.0.123 / 9.0.320](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/9.0/9.0.22/9.0.22.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/9.0))
* [.NET 10.0.14 and .NET SDK 10.0.114 / 10.0.403](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/10.0/10.0.14/10.0.14.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/10.0))
* [.NET 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 and .NET SDK 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 (prerelease)](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc3/11.0.0-rc.3.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/11.0))

## Security advisories

| Advisory | Applicability | Announcement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [CVE-2026-111497](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/security/advisories/GHSA-p3jp-9v83-76w9) | Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write; all platforms when processing untrusted Brotli data. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494) |
| [CVE-2026-114148](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/security/advisories/GHSA-r6pf-x897-gm86) | Linux archive ownership; distribution-specific ASP.NET Core archives and source-build engineering inputs. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/495) |
| [CVE-2026-70197](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/security/advisories/GHSA-4mpw-cpwj-hxxj) | Windows sockets memory corruption; corrected October 13 fix. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/493) |
| [CVE-2026-102870](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/security/advisories/GHSA-g27p-qf6j-c96c) | Standalone Blazor WebAssembly debugger packages on .NET 10/11; corrected October 13 fix. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/492) |

The October 13 updates did not fully address CVE-2026-70197 and CVE-2026-102870. These out-of-band updates provide the corrected fixes; the original advisory identities and revision history are preserved. For CVE-2026-102870, update the affected standalone Server/DevServer package references; updating only the shared runtime is not a substitute.

For CVE-2026-114148, affected Microsoft-published .NET 8/9 ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarball installations require a clean replacement following the advisory. Source-built archives are build/engineering inputs, not directly deployed production runtimes. Update those inputs and recreate their extracted workspaces using ownership-controlled extraction; review and rebuild affected downstream outputs as needed. .NET 10/11 applicability is limited to source-built distributions.

Also announced at [.NET October 2026 Out-of-Band Security Updates](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/dotnet-october-2026-oob-security-updates/).

Please use the [release feedback issue](https://github.com/dotnet/core/issues/10660) for release-wide issues and the linked per-CVE discussions for advisory questions.

Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-114148 | .NET Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in file ownership in Linux .NET tarball distributions, including ASP.NET Core runtime tarballs, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack tarballs, and source-built .NET tarballs. This advisory also provides guidance on updating affected installations and source-build engineering workflows. Incorrect ownership of runtime files installed from affected Linux tarballs can allow local elevation of privilege. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/70040 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-276 (Incorrect Default Permissions) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Linux - **Architectures:** ARM, ARM64 and x64, as applicable to the affected Linux distribution. ## Affected Products The affected ASP.NET Core runtime, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack, and source-built .NET Linux tarballs are listed below. The installation and source-build engineering scenarios require different remediation, as described in [How do I fix the issue?](#how-fix). ### Microsoft-published ASP.NET Core archives For Microsoft-published .NET 8 and .NET 9 distributions, only the ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarballs are affected. Other Microsoft-published .NET runtime and SDK tarballs are not included in this scope. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- ASP.NET Core 8 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 8 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 9 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 ASP.NET Core 9 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 These products use the archive names `aspnetcore-runtime-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, `aspnetcore-runtime-composite-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, and `aspnetcore-targeting-pack-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, where `{rid}` is `linux-arm`, `linux-arm64`, `linux-x64`, `linux-musl-arm`, `linux-musl-arm64` or `linux-musl-x64`. Runtime tarballs are listed on the [.NET download site](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet); targeting-pack tarballs are distributed through the .NET download CDN. ### Source-built distributions Every tarball type produced by source-build is affected in the ranges below, not only SDK tarballs. The versions in this table identify the corresponding source-build SDK release. Source-built tarballs are used in build and engineering workflows, rather than deployed directly to customer installations. Consuming an affected source-build archive does not, by itself, mean that a production shared runtime was installed from that archive. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- Source-built .NET 8 Linux distributions | >= 8.0.100, < 8.0.133 | 8.0.133 Source-built .NET 9 Linux distributions | >= 9.0.100, < 9.0.123 | 9.0.123 Source-built .NET 10.0.1xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.100, <= 10.0.113 | 10.0.114-servicing.26522.126 Source-built .NET 10.0.4xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.400, <= 10.0.402 | 10.0.403-servicing.26523.112 Source-built .NET 11 preview Linux distributions | >= 11.0.100-preview.1.26104.118, <= 11.0.100-rc.2.26504.105 | 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Review whether an installation came from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, or whether a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built archive. Check whether extraction preserved numeric ownership and whether the resulting files have the intended ownership. A .NET version number alone does not identify which archive was used or establish the ownership of an installation or build workspace. The vulnerability can affect installations that preserve numeric file ownership from an affected archive, for example during privileged extraction or ownership-preserving container archive import. A local account that controls the installed files or writable directories may be able to modify files used by a more privileged application. Restoring ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack NuGet packages does not, by itself, introduce this tarball ownership defect. Applications using a shared runtime installed from an affected tarball can still be affected. ### How do I fix the issue? #### Customer-deployed installations For an installation made from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, replace the affected installation with a clean installation from the patched distribution listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Updating a NuGet reference, downloading a new archive, or extracting over an existing installation does not by itself correct the existing installation. 1. Identify the affected installation directories and the applications, services, scheduled jobs, and container images that use them. Stop affected applications and services before switching installations. 2. Obtain the patched archives appropriate to your distribution, architecture, and required components from the trusted publisher. Verify their checksums against the publisher's trusted release information before extracting them. 3. Install into a **new, empty directory**, not the affected installation tree. For a shared or privileged installation, use a trusted administrator account and an administrator-controlled directory whose parent directories cannot be modified by untrusted accounts. Do not copy binaries, plugins, or other files from the affected tree into the replacement. Install any required side-by-side versions from trusted, fixed distributions. 4. Extract without restoring the archive's user/group ownership. Follow the [manual installation guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/install/linux-scripted-manual#manual-install), which uses `--no-same-owner`. For GNU tar, the following example also applies a restrictive write-permission mask: ```bash ( umask 022 tar -xzf "$PATCHED_ARCHIVE" -C "$NEW_DOTNET_ROOT" \ --no-same-owner --no-same-permissions ) ``` `PATCHED_ARCHIVE` must identify the verified patched archive, and `NEW_DOTNET_ROOT` must identify the new, empty installation directory. For a shared or privileged installation, run extraction in the trusted administrator context. Confirm that the resulting files, directories, and parent directories are controlled by the intended trusted owner and cannot be modified by untrusted accounts, including through group permissions or access-control lists. 5. Update application and service configuration to use the replacement installation, then restart and verify the applications. Check the actual runtime selected by each application, not only the version reported by an unrelated `dotnet` executable on `PATH`. Ensure that no service, scheduled job, or runtime search path still selects the affected installation. Retire the old tree using your deployment procedures, preserving evidence first if compromise is suspected. 6. Rebuild affected custom container images from trusted inputs using the patched archives and ownership-controlled extraction, and deploy replacement containers. Changing only a running container does not correct the image used to create subsequent containers. #### Source-build engineering workflows If a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built tarball, update that input to the patched source-build release listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Recreate its extracted workspace in a new, trusted directory using ownership-controlled extraction, rather than reusing a tree extracted from the affected archive. The extraction guidance above also applies to these workspaces. Review downstream runtime or SDK packages and custom images for ownership inherited from the affected archive, and rebuild affected outputs as needed. The customer-installation steps above apply if affected outputs were actually installed or deployed; do not treat the source-build engineering archive itself as a deployed production runtime. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind. Microsoft disclaims all warranties, either express or implied, including the warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose. In no event shall Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers be liable for any damages whatsoever including direct, indirect, incidental, consequential, loss of business profits or special damages, even if Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers have been advised of the possibility of such damages. Some states do not allow the exclusion or limitation of liability for consequential or incidental damages so the foregoing limitation may not apply. ### External Links [CVE-2026-114148](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-114148) ### Acknowledgements - Alen Cheung ### Revisions V1.0 (10/25/2026): Initial advisory.

Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 | .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136446 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below. ### .NET 8 Package name | Affected version | Patched version ------------ | ---------------- | --------------- 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 | 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in [affected packages](#affected-packages), including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See [mitigations](#mitigations) for the affected usage paths and default settings. ### How do I fix the issue? Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above. .NET release | Runtime | SDK versions ------------ | ------- | ------------ .NET 8 | 8.0.33 | 8.0.133, 8.0.427 .NET 9 | 9.0.22 | 9.0.123, 9.0.320 .NET 10 | 10.0.14 | 10.0.114, 10.0.403 .NET 11 previews | 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 | 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet. * If you're using .NET 8.0, you should download and install .NET 8.0.33 Runtime or .NET 8.0.133 or 8.0.427 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/8.0. * If you're using .NET 9.0, you should download and install .NET 9.0.22 Runtime or .NET 9.0.123 or 9.0.320 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/9.0. * If you're using .NET 10.0, you should download and install .NET 10.0.14 Runtime or .NET 10.0.114 or 10.0.403 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/10.0. * If you're using .NET 11.0, you should download and install .NET 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 Runtime or .NET 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/11.0. Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect. If you have deployed [self-contained applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/deploying/#self-contained-deployments), rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime. For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind. Some states do not allow the exclusion or limitation of liability for consequential or incidental damages so the foregoing limitation may not apply. ### External Links [CVE-2026-111497](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-111497) ### Revisions V1.0 (10/25/2026): Initial advisory.

Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-70197 | .NET and Visual Studio Remote Code Execution Vulnerability | October 25, 2026 OOB update
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in System.Net.Sockets. This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability. On Windows, reusing a `SocketAsyncEventArgs` instance across IPv4 and IPv6 datagram sockets can retain an undersized cached native address buffer, allowing an unauthenticated out-of-bounds write during `ReceiveFromAsync`. This vulnerability was disclosed in the October 13 advisory, but the fix was not included in the previous updates. This revision provides the corrected packages under the existing CVE-2026-70197. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136445 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Windows - **Architectures:** All ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects Microsoft .NET projects that use an affected package version listed below. Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-102870 | ASP.NET Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability | October 25, 2026 OOB update
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in the Blazor WebAssembly debugger included in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server`. This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability. `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer` also bundles the affected debugger. The Blazor WebAssembly debug proxy evaluates debugger expressions by generating and compiling C# source. Certain values originating in the application being debugged, including `ToString()` results, descriptions, and class names, are embedded in that generated source without consistent escaping. An attacker-controlled value can escape the generated string literal and execute code on a developer's machine when the developer evaluates an expression during debugging. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/70039 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-94 (Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Windows, Linux, macOS - **Architectures:** All ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects Microsoft .NET projects that use an affected package version listed below. You are affected if you use a vulnerable version of `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server` or `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer` to debug a Blazor WebAssembly application and evaluate an expression involving attacker-controlled application data. ### How do I fix the issue? 1. Install the latest supported version of .NET. 2. Update each affected `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server` or `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer` package reference to the patched version for the .NET release used by the application. Updating only the shared runtime is not a substitute for updating these standalone packages. Once the updated packages are installed, restart the debugger and development environment. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Issues.Title: .NET 11 Release Candidate 2
Issues.Body:
> This issue is a locked mirror of [dotnet/core/discussions/10644](https://github.com/dotnet/core/discussions/10644). See that thread for discussion.

We are pleased to announce the release of .NET 11 Release Candidate 2. Follow the main announcement and [blog announcement](https://aka.ms/dotnet/11/rc2).

This is our second of two release candidates which come with a [go-live support license](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/platform/support/policy/dotnet-core#previews) so you can confidently use this release for your production applications. This release of .NET 11 is supported in the new [Visual Studio 2026 Insiders](https://visualstudio.microsoft.com/insiders/) release alongside Visual Studio Code with the C# Dev Kit. Check out the full release notes below and get started today.

This release contains the following highlights and improvements.

Browse the release notes for a full list of improvements in this release:

- [.NET MAUI](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/dotnetmaui.md)
- [ASP.NET Core](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/aspnetcore.md)
- [C#](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/csharp.md)
- [F#](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/fsharp.md)
- [Container images](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/containers.md)
- [EF Core & Data](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/efcore.md)
- [Libraries](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/libraries.md)
- [MSBuild](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/msbuild.md)
- [NuGet](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/nuget.md)
- [Runtime](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/runtime.md)
- [SDK](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/sdk.md)
- [Windows Forms](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/winforms.md)

## Get started

To get started with .NET 11, [install the .NET 11 SDK](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/11.0).

If you're on Windows using Visual Studio, we recommend installing the latest [Visual Studio 2026 Insiders](https://visualstudio.microsoft.com/insiders/). You can also use Visual Studio Code and the [C# Dev Kit](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-dotnettools.csdevkit) extension with .NET 11.

Crafted WPF pixel-shader bytecode can desynchronize the two parsing passes in `CPSTrans::Initialize`, causing heap out-of-bounds writes or reads. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/wpf/issues/12026 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Windows - **Architectures:** All ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects Microsoft .NET projects that use an affected package version listed below. Package name | Affected version | Patched version ------------ | ---------------- | --------------- [Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-arm64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-arm64) | >= 8.0.0, <= 8.0.31 | 8.0.32 [Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-x64) | >= 8.0.0, <= 8.0.31 | 8.0.32 [Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-x64) | >= 11.0.0-preview.1, <= 11.0.0-rc.1 | 11.0.0-rc.2 [Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-x86](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-x86) | >= 11.0.0-preview.1, <= 11.0.0-rc.1 | 11.0.0-rc.2 [Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-arm64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-arm64) | >= 9.0.0, <= 9.0.20 | 9.0.21 [Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-x64) | >= 9.0.0, <= 9.0.20 | 9.0.21 [Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-x86](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-x86) | >= 9.0.0, <= 9.0.20 | 9.0.21 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? If using a package listed in [affected packages](#affected-packages), you're exposed to the vulnerability. ### How do I fix the issue? 1. To fix the issue please install the latest version of .NET. If you have installed one or more .NET SDKs through Visual Studio, Visual Studio will prompt you to update Visual Studio, which will also update your .NET SDKs. 2. If your application references the vulnerable package, update the package reference to the patched version. You can list the versions you have installed by running the `dotnet --info` command. * If you're using .NET 8.0, you should download and install .NET 8.0.32 Runtime or .NET 8.0.426 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/8.0. * If you're using .NET 9.0, you should download and install .NET 9.0.21 Runtime or .NET 9.0.319 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/9.0. * If you're using .NET 10.0, you should download and install .NET 10.0.13 Runtime or .NET 10.0.402 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/10.0. * If you're using .NET 11.0, you should download and install .NET 11.0.0-rc.2 Runtime or .NET 11.0.100-rc.2 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/11.0. Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect. Additionally, if you've deployed [self-contained applications](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/deploying/#self-contained-deployments-scd) targeting any of the impacted versions, these applications are also vulnerable and must be recompiled and redeployed. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/wpf. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind.
